unlisted_practices: Professional medical associations and provincial medical colleges should develop guidance for physicians on the use of AI-powered symptom checker apps, including factors for determining which apps are safe, reliable, and as free of discriminatory outcomes as possible.
Medical colleges should provide guidance for physicians on whether and how to recommend AI symptom checker apps to their patients.
Medical colleges should provide guidance on how physicians should manage information from an AI symptom checker app when a patient presents with a mobile-mediated diagnosis.
Regulators should establish a system of regulation and guidance for AI symptom checker apps that empowers users to decide which apps are safe and reliable and delineates clinician responsibilities.
Regulators should periodically review individual AI symptom checker apps to ensure they continue to function properly.
Developers should embed technical safeguards in AI symptom checker apps to mitigate or correct biased outcomes, without relying on them alone.
Developers should train AI symptom checkers principally on unbiased or neutral data.
Researchers should continue to monitor the quality, safety, and efficacy of AI symptom checker apps.
Physicians should use mobile health apps only to complement, never replace, physician care, and should prescribe apps primarily to enhance the safety or effectiveness of patient care.
Trusted sources should provide lists of mobile health apps evaluated for safety and efficacy to help clinicians select apps.
Organizations should provide clinicians with mobile health training.

screen.reason: This is an ethical and legal commentary/analysis examining AI symptom checker apps (focusing on Babylon and Ada) regarding entrenched bias, regulation, and professional responsibility.
